entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.1-1Chr.29.2">1Ch 29:1-2</reference> <hi type="italic">Contributions of the collected princes for the building of the temple</hi>. - David then turns to the assembled princes to press upon them the furthering of the building of the temple. After referring to the youth of his son, and to the greatness of the work to be accomplished (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.1">1Ch 29:1</reference>), he mentions what materials he has prepared for the building of the temple (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.2">1Ch 29:2</reference>); then further states what he has resolved to give in addition from his private resources (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.4">1Ch 29:4</reference>); and finally, after this introduction, calls upon those present to make a voluntary collection for this great work (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.5">1Ch 29:5</reference>). The words, “as only one hath God chosen him,” form a parenthesis, which is to be translated as a relative sentence for “my son, whom alone God hath chosen.” ורך נער as in 1Ch 22:5. The work is great, because not for man the palace, <hi type="italic">scil.</hi> is intended, i.e., shall be built, but for Jahve God. הבּירה, the citadel, the palace; a later word, generally used of the residence of the Persian king (<reference osisRef="Esth.1.2">Est 1:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Esth.1.5">Est 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.2.3">Est 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.1.1">Neh 1:1</reference>), only in <reference osisRef="Neh.2.8">Neh 2:8</reference> of the citadel by the temple; here transferred to the temple as the glorious palace of Jahve, the God-king of Israel. With <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Chr.29.2">1Ch 29:2</reference></hi>, cf. 1Ch 22:14. וגו לזּהב הזּהב, the gold for the golden, etc., i.e., for the vessels and ornaments of gold, cf. 1Ch 28:14. וּמלּוּאים שׁהם אבני as in <reference osisRef="Exod.25.7">Exo 25:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.35.9">Exo 35:9</reference>, precious stones for the ephod and choshen. שׁהם, probably beryl. מּלּוּאים אבני, stones of filling, that is, precious stones which are put in settings. פּוּך אבני, stones of pigment, i.e., ornament, conjecturally precious stones which, from their black colour, were in appearance like פּוּך, <hi type="italic">stibium</hi>, a common eye pigment (see 2Ki 9:30). רקמה אבני, stones of variegated colour, i.e., with veins of different colours. יקרה אבן, precious stones, according to <reference osisRef="2Chr.3.6">2Ch 3:6</reference>, for ornamenting the walls. שׁישׁ אבני, white marble stones.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.5">1Ch 29:5</reference> לזּהב לזּהב, for every golden thing, etc., cf. 1Ch 29:2. וּלכל־מלאכה, and in general for every work to be wrought by the hands of the artificer. וּמי, who then is willing (uw expressing it as the consequence). To fill one’s hand to the Lord, means to provide oneself with something which one brings to the Lord; see on Exo 32:29. The infinitive מלּאות occurs also in <reference osisRef="Exod.31.5">Exo 31:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.9.4">Dan 9:4</reference>, and along with מלּא,   2Ch 13:9.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.6-1Chr.29.8">1Ch 29:6-8</reference> <div eID="gen5901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5902" type="x-p"/> The princes follow the example, and willingly respond to David’s call. האבות שׂרי = האבות ראשׁי,   <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.31">1Ch 24:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.1">1Ch 27:1</reference>, etc. הם מלאכת ולשׂרי, and as regards the princes of the work of the king. The למּלך וּמקנה רכוּשׁ שׂרי, <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.1">1Ch 28:1</reference>, the officials enumerated in <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.25-1Chr.27.31">1Ch 27:25-31</reference> are meant; on ל see on 1Ch 28:21. They gave 5000 talents of gold (22 1/2 or 11 1/2 millions of pounds), and 1000 darics = 11 1/2 millions of pounds. אדרכּון, with א <hi type="italic">prosth</hi>. here and in Ezr 8:27, and דּרכּמון, Ezr 2:69; Neh 7:70., does not correspond to the Greek δραχμή, Arab. <hi type="italic">dirhem</hi>, but to the Greek δαρεικός, as the Syrian translation <hi type="italic">derîkônā'</hi>, Ezr 8:27, shows; a Persian gold coin worth about 22s. 6d. See the description of these coins, of which several specimens still exist, in Cavedoni <hi type="italic">bibl. Numismatik, übers</hi>. von A. Werlhof, S. 84ff.; J. Brandis, <hi type="italic">das Münz-Mass und Gewishtssystem in Vorderasien</hi> (1866), S. 244; and my <hi type="italic">bibl. Archäol</hi>. §127, 3. “Our historian uses the words used in his time to designate the current gold coins, without intending to assume that there were darics in use in the time of David, to state in a way intelligible to his readers the amount of the sum contributed by the princes” (Bertheau). This perfectly correct remark does not, however, explain why the author of the Chronicle has stated the contribution in gold and that in silver in different values, in talents and in darics, since the second cannot be an explanation of the first, the two sums being different. Probably the sum in darics is the amount which they contributed in gold pieces received as coins; the talents, on the other hand, probably represent the weight of the vessels and other articles of gold which they brought as offerings for the building. The amount contributed in silver is not large when compared with that in gold: 10,000 talents = £3,500,000, or one half that amount. The contribution in copper also, 18,000 talents, is not very large. Besides these, those who had stones, i.e., precious stones, also brought them. אתּו הנּמצא, that was found with him, for: that which he (each one) had of stones they gave. The sing. אתּו is to be taken distributively, and is consequently carried on in the plural, נתנוּ; cf. Ew. §319, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. אבנים is <hi type="italic">accus</hi>. of subordination. יד על נתן, to give over for administration (Ew. §282, <hi type="italic">b</hi>). יחיאל, the Levite family of this name which had the oversight of the treasures of the house of God (1Ch 26:21.).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.10-1Chr.29.11">1Ch 29:10-11</reference> <hi type="italic">David’s thanksgiving prayer</hi>. - David gives fitting expression to his joy on the success of the deepest wish of his heart, in a prayer with which he closes the last parliament of his reign. Since according to the divine decree, not he, the man of war, but his son, the peace-king Solomon, was to build a temple to the Lord, David had taken it upon himself to prepare as far as possible for the carrying out of the work. He had also found the princes and chiefs of the people willing to further it, and to assist his son Solomon in it. In this the pious and grey-haired servant of the Lord saw a special proof of the divine favour, for which he must thank God the Lord before the whole congregation. He praises Jahve, “the God of Israel our father,” <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.10">1Ch 29:10</reference>, or, as it is in <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.18">1Ch 29:18</reference>, “the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob, our fathers.” Jahve had clearly revealed himself to David and his people as the God of Israel and of the patriarchs, by fulfilling in so glorious a manner to the people of Israel, by David, the promises made to the patriarchs. God the Lord had not only by David made His people great and powerful, and secured to them the peaceful possession of the good land, by humbling all their enemies round about, but He had also awakened in the heart of the people such love to and trust in their God, that the assembled dignitaries of the kingdom showed themselves perfectly willing to assist in furthering the building of the house of God. In this God had revealed His greatness, power, glory, etc., as David (in <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.11">1Ch 29:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.12">1Ch 29:12</reference>) acknowledges with praise: “Thine, Jahve, is the greatness,” etc. הנּצח, according to the Aramaic usage, gloria, splendour, honour. כל כּי, yea all, still dependent on לך at the commencement of the sentence, so that we do not need to supply לך after כּי. “Thine is the dominion, and the raising of oneself to be head over all.” In His ממלכה God reveals His greatness, might, glory, etc. ממנשּׂא is not a participle requiring אתּה, “thou art,” to be supplied (Berth.), but an appellative, an Aramaic infinitive, - the raising oneself (Ew. §160, <hi type="italic">e</hi>).

In this God had revealed His greatness, power, glory, etc., as David (in 1Ch 29:11 , 1Ch 29:12 ) acknowledges with praise: “Thine, Jahve, is the greatness,” etc. הנּצח, according to the Aramaic usage, gloria, splendour, honour. כל כּי, yea all, still dependent on לך at the commencement of the sentence, so that we do not need to supply לך after כּי. “Thine is the dominion, and the raising of oneself to be head over all.” In His ממלכה God reveals His greatness, might, glory, etc. ממנשּׂא is not a participle requiring אתּה, “thou art,” to be supplied (Berth.), but an appellative, an Aramaic infinitive, - the raising oneself (Ew. §160, e ).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.21">1Ch 29:21</reference> <div eID="gen5910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5911" type="x-p"/> To seal their confession, thus made in word and deed, the assembled dignitaries prepared a great sacrificial feast to the Lord on the following day. They sacrificed to the Lord sacrifices, viz., 1000 bullocks, 1000 rams, and 1000 lambs as burnt-offering, with drink-offerings to correspond, and sacrifices, i.e., thank-offerings (שׁלמים), in multitude for all Israel, i.e., so that all those present could take part in the sacrificial meal prepared from these sacrifices. While זבהים in the first clause is the general designation of the bloody offerings as distinguished from the meat-offerings, in the last clause it is restricted by the contrast with עלות and the שׁלמים, from which joyous sacrificial meals were prepared.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.23-1Chr.29.24">1Ch 29:23-24</reference> <hi type="italic">Solomon’s accession and David’s death</hi>, with a statement as to the length of his reign and the sources of the history. - <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.23">1Ch 29:23</reference>-25. The remarks on Solomon’s accession and reign contained in these verses are necessary to the complete conclusion of a history of David’s reign, for they show how David’s wishes for his son Solomon, whom Jahve chose to be his successor, were fulfilled. On יהוה על־כּסּא see the commentary on 1Ch 28:5. ויּצלח, he was prosperous, corresponds to the hope expressed by David (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.13">1Ch 22:13</reference>), which was also fulfilled by the submission of all princes and heroes, and also of all the king’s sons, to King Solomon (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.24">1Ch 29:24</reference>). There can hardly, however, be in these last words a reference to the frustrating of Adonijah’s attempted usurpation of the throne (cf. 1Ki 1:15.). תּחת יד נתן = to submit. But this meaning is not derived (Rashi) from the custom of taking oaths of fidelity by clasping of hands, for this custom cannot be certainly proved to have existed among the Israelites; still less can it have arisen from the ancient custom mentioned in <reference osisRef="Gen.24.2">Gen 24:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.9">Gen 24:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.47.29">Gen 47:29</reference>, of laying the hand under the thigh of the person to whom one swore in making promises with oath. The hand, as the instrument of all activity, is here simply a symbol of power.

1Ch 29:29-30 

 On the authorities cited see the Introduction. וגו כּל־מלכוּתו עם goes with כּתוּבים הנּם: the acts of David ... are written ... together with his whole reign and his power, and the times which went over him. העתּים, the times, with their joys and sorrows, as in Psa 31:16 ; Job 24:1. The kingdoms of the lands (cf. 2Ch 12:8 ; 2Ch 17:10 ; 2Ch 20:29 ) are the kingdoms with which the Israelites under David came into contact-Philistia, Edom, Moab, Ammon, Aram.
